titre_video: The Nuclear Football is BROKEN. It's JUST 4 Minutes to WW3

segments.titre: Hook: the red button is a lie and the 360-second clock
segments.resume: The video opens by claiming the world is minutes from annihilation and that the President's red button is a lie. The real system is a ticking clock giving one person only 360 seconds to decide on a strike that would kill hundreds of millions.
segments.texte: Right now, the world is just minutes away from total annihilation. The red button on the President’s desk is a lie. The real system is a ticking clock and it’s already running down When humanity is standing on the brink of total destruction, one person must make a decision that will vaporize hundreds of millions of people. And they only have 360 seconds to choose.

segments.titre: The Football: the Presidential Emergency Satchel
segments.resume: At 3:04 am the Pentagon calls the Executive residence with an incoming missile warning, and an aide brings a 45-pound black briefcase. Officially the Presidential Emergency Satchel, it follows every president around the clock, got the nickname the Football from the war plan code-named Dropkick, and is built to eliminate hesitation.
segments.texte: T-06:00 3.04 am. A phone screams in the Executive residence. A breathless voice from the Pentagon is on the other end. It’s the nightmare scenario no President wants to hear: Incoming nuclear missiles have been detected. The countdown is live. The first thing the President doesn’t do, is reach for the “nuclear button”. It doesn’t exist. Instead, a military officer bursts into the room carrying a 45 pound (20 kg) black leather briefcase. The aide carrying it is a rotating officer from 1 of the 5 service branches. They shadow the commander-in-chief constantly. They’re never more than a few steps away, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, every single day of a presidency. That briefcase has followed every American president for more than 60 years. It rides in the same motorcade, boards the same plane, waits outside the same rooms… it’s always within reach. The official name is the Presidential Emergency Satchel. Everyone who works around it calls it the Football. The name traces back to an early nuclear war plan with the code name "Dropkick,” football being the obvious shorthand. Inside is a bureaucratic machine assembled across six decades, built out of laminated cards and encrypted radio signals. And it’s designed to do one thing: eliminate hesitation. And hesitate is the one thing the President can’t do right now.

segments.titre: What the Football contains: identity, comms and the menu
segments.resume: The Football locks the president's identity to the National Military Command Center, provides secure communications for a launch order, and holds a simplified menu of strike options. Garrett Graff and Colonel Buzz Patterson describe the laminated guide as a Denny's or Chinese-restaurant menu, and there is no red button or retina scanner, only a credit-card-sized card.
segments.texte: T-05:30 The officer slams the briefcase down on a desk and rips open the zippers as the seconds tick away. The President fights the grogginess and prepares for the most important decision in human history. The Football does three things. First, it locks in the president’s identity to the National Military Command Center at the Pentagon. Second, it provides secure communications to initiate a launch order. And third, it contains a simplified menu of nuclear strike options. Journalist Garrett Graff, who wrote a definitive account of the Football for CNN, reported that aides have described a laminated visual guide inside the briefcase as looking like a "Denny's menu" of nuclear war. Military aide and Air Force Colonel Buzz Patterson, who carried the Football for President Clinton, described the selection process as "picking one [menu option] out of Column A and two out of Column B," like ordering at a Chinese restaurant. Each option represents a different scale of nuclear destruction. Everything from a limited strike to something that eliminates entire regions of the planet. There’s no retina scanner inside the Football. There’s no “red button.” All it takes is a single piece of plastic, roughly the size of a credit card. And that card has the potential to be the most dangerous object in the world. Without it… America is about to be a radioactive wasteland.

segments.titre: The missing Biscuit: Carter's dry cleaning and Reagan's shooting
segments.resume: The President cannot find the Biscuit, the card with the Gold Codes that the Pentagon needs before it will fire. Jimmy Carter once sent his Biscuit to the dry cleaner in a suit, and after John Hinckley shot Reagan in March 1981 the card was left in a shoe at George Washington University Hospital and returned two days later by the FBI.
segments.texte: T-05:00 The President throws back the bedsheets. He scrambles blindly for the small laminated card, known as the Biscuit or the Gold Codes. Whatever its name… it’s not there. All the President finds is empty wood. To authorize the end of the world, the President has to read the codes printed on the card. Without them, the Pentagon will refuse to fire. A cold sweat breaks across his forehead. This isn’t a drill… It’s history repeating itself. Decades earlier, Jimmy Carter, a former nuclear submarine engineer, demanded the nuclear protocol to be simplified. The original process was too slow, too wieldy to survive a nuclear attack. So, the Biscuit was born. Then Carter put it into a suit pocket and sent it to the dry cleaner. While a hypothetical nuclear countdown was ticking, the literal key to the nuclear arsenal was spinning around a washing machine. Ronald Reagan’s situation was infinitely darker. In March 1981, John Hinckley shot Reagan outside the Washington Hilton Hotel. As doctors frantically cut the President’s clothes off in the emergency room no one thought to secure the Biscuit. It was eventually tucked into one of Reagan’s shoes in the trauma bay in George Washington University Hospital. The FBI eventually found it and returned it to the White House… 2 days later. None of that matters to the current President. All he knows is that America is on the verge of being wiped out. And the clock is ticking…

segments.titre: Finding the Biscuit and rushing to the bunker
segments.resume: The President finds the Biscuit in a suit jacket pocket, but the Pentagon line is dead with static. Secret Service agents rush him with the Football through a corridor, elevator and reinforced blast doors.
segments.texte: T-04:30 The President springs from the bed and rummages through drawers. Aides upend furniture. Then the President’s fingers feel cold hard plastic. Buried in a pocket of a suit jacket… the Biscuit. He pulls it out, cracks the plastic and stares at the authentication codes. An aide holds a phone… he’s met with static. The Pentagon is out of reach. Just then, Secret Service agents burst into the Presidential bedroom. They grab the President and barrel him down a corridor, into an elevator and through reinforced doors. The Football follows him. The heavy blast doors slam shut sealing them all inside with a metallic thud.

segments.titre: ICBM versus submarine-launched missile warning times
segments.resume: An ICBM from Russia takes about 26 to 30 minutes and is detected immediately by satellites thanks to its heat signature, while submarine-launched missiles can arrive in 15 or even 10 minutes. A 1982 Joint Chiefs of Staff study found only about 3.5 minutes in some SLBM scenarios, so command centers could be destroyed before the President decides.
segments.texte: When an intercontinental ballistic missile launches from Russian soil, it takes roughly 26 to 30 minutes to reach the continental United States. That buys time to think and verify and consult. But ICBM launches are detectable from the moment of launch thanks to their enormous heat signatures. They’re picked up immediately from surveillance satellites. But Submarine-launched ballistic missiles? They’re different. An enemy submarine can position itself hundreds of miles off the American coastline without detection. A missile launched from that position has more like 15 minutes of travel time. If the submarine is positioned close enough, the window of detection and impact collapses to somewhere closer to 10. But a 1982 Joint Chiefs of Staff historical study exposed an even more brutal reality. In certain SLBM scenarios, there can be about 3 and a half minutes between the moment a missile breaks the surface and direct strikes on the nation's command centers. The entire command structure can be obliterated before it has a chance to decide how to respond. Which means by the time the President reads his identification codes, the room he’s standing in might already be gone.

segments.titre: Verifying the attack: NORAD, STRATCOM and the confidence level
segments.resume: Early warning teams at NORAD, STRATCOM and the National Military Command Center calculate trajectories and assign a low, medium or high confidence level. The STRATCOM commander briefs the President on the threat, the response options and the civilian casualties of each.
segments.texte: T-04:00 The atmosphere crackles. The President and his aides frantically try to reconnect with the Pentagon. As the missiles move closer, information travels at the speed of light to early warning teams at NORAD in Colorado, U.S. Strategic Command in Nebraska, and the National Military Command Center at the Pentagon. Analysts pull up the tracking data. They calculate the trajectory, and assign a confidence level Low, medium, or high. That was why the President was woken up at 3:04 a.m. The STRATCOM commander briefs the President on the threat, the available response options, and what each option means in terms of civilian casualties on both sides.

segments.resume: In January 1995 Russian radar detected a rocket off Norway that resembled a Trident missile, but it was a Black Brant XII aurora research rocket whose launch notice never reached radar operators. Yeltsin's Cheget briefcase was activated for the first time in a real emergency until the rocket curved out to sea at minute eight.
segments.texte: The President’s mind races. Could it be a mistake? It’s happened before. Back in January 1995, Russian scientists at an early warning radar station in the northwestern part of the country detected an unidentified rocket rising somewhere off the Norwegian coast. The radar track showed the missile ascending on a trajectory that was nearly identical to a U.S. Trident submarine missile. The kind that could be used to blind Russian radar and command systems before a larger first strike. Russian military protocols activated immediately. But what the radar operators did not know was that Norwegian and American scientists had just launched a four-stage Black Brant XII research rocket to study the aurora borealis. They had notified 30 countries in advance, including Russia. The Russian Foreign Ministry received the notification. The information never made it to the radar technicians. An anonymous Russian general later explained that officials had taken "a literal attitude" toward the notice, assuming it was meant for sailors, not military personnel. For the next eight minutes, Russian radar tracked the rocket. Protocol required a decision to be made before the decision window closed. A real Trident from the Barents Sea would reach mainland Russia in approximately 10 minutes. Russian submarine commanders were ordered into combat readiness. Boris Yeltsin, the President of Russia, was notified and his Cheget, Russia's nuclear briefcase equivalent, was activated. It was the first and only time in recorded history that a Russian president's nuclear briefcase had ever been turned on in a genuine emergency. Yeltsin had to decide whether to initiate a retaliatory nuclear strike against the United States. At minute eight, Russian observers determined the rocket was curving away from Russian territory. It was heading toward the open sea. The alert was stood down. This time, the President might not be so lucky.

segments.titre: Bruce Blair: six minutes and the incapacitated President
segments.resume: Ground radar confirms the attack with a second independent system. Former Minuteman launch officer Bruce Blair says the president has roughly six minutes and the process is rushed and mechanical, exposing the flaw of an irrational, panicking or incapacitated president.
segments.texte: T-03:30 Ground-based radar systems confirm that the missiles are in mid-flight. The attack is now verified by a second independent system. The situation is terrifyingly real. Nuclear security expert and former Minuteman ICBM launch officer Bruce Blair, a man who spent a career studying the system from the inside, put it directly: “The president has roughly six minutes to make a decision if it appears that we are under attack." He added that "The whole process is very rushed and very mechanical.” That’s just the physics of nuclear retaliation. But Blair also exposed a huge flaw. One that was swept under the rug during the cold war. What if the President acts irrational or panic stricken? Even worse, what if they’re already incapacitated?

segments.titre: Perimeter, the Soviet Dead Hand system
segments.resume: In 1985 the Soviet Union activated Perimeter, nicknamed Dead Hand, to preserve retaliation under Mutually Assured Destruction if leadership was wiped out. It monitors seismic activity, radiation, pressure and heat, and can launch a command rocket that broadcasts launch orders to all surviving nuclear forces, and it is thought to be still operational.
segments.texte: The Soviets already had the answer for that back in 1985, the Soviet Union quietly activated a system they called Perimeter. In the West, it earned another nickname. “The Dead Hand.” It was built on an assumption of what might happen if American missiles destroyed Soviet leadership so completely and quickly that nobody survived to authorize retaliation. The entire political stability of Mutually Assured Destruction, or MAD, depends on both sides being able to respond. If you could decapitate the Soviet command structure in a surprise first strike, MAD breaks down. The threat of retaliation disappears, because there’s nobody left to retaliate. Dead Hand was the answer to that problem. It's a system that monitors seismic activity, radiation levels, air pressure, and heat across the Russian territory. If those sensors pick up patterns consistent with nuclear detonations, and if the command structure is incapacitated, Dead Hand can autonomously launch a command rocket. That command rocket carries a radio transmitter rather than a warhead. It broadcasts launch orders to every surviving Russian nuclear asset on the ground, including silos, submarines, and mobile launchers. Even if every human in the Russian chain of command has been killed, the missiles launch. Perimeter became operational in 1985 and, based on available evidence, has remained operational into the present day. Whatever happens… the missiles are coming.

segments.resume: Humanity is trapped in a six-minute nightmare because of the Launch on Warning doctrine: if an attack is detected, missiles are launched before enemy warheads land. The logic is that ICBMs in fixed silos are vulnerable, so weapons must be launched early to survive.
segments.texte: T-03:00 The clock is ticking. Red lights strobe across the secure White House bunker. Aides frantically scream into phones. Monitors track a cluster of red plumes arcing over the northern hemisphere. Humanity is trapped in a 6 minute nightmare. And most people don’t even realize how we got here. The answer lies in a military doctrine most people have never heard of, called Launch on Warning. It’s simple in concept, but apocalyptic in execution. If you detect an incoming attack, you launch your missiles before the enemy's missiles land. The reasoning is straightforward. ICBMs in fixed silos are vulnerable to incoming warheads. If you wait to absorb a first strike before retaliating, your arsenal might already be destroyed. So you launch early. You keep your weapons alive by getting them off the ground before the enemy's weapons arrive.

segments.titre: The US has no Dead Hand: sole presidential authority
segments.resume: The United States is not known to have a Dead Hand system, and a nuclear launch depends solely on the commander in chief. No one else has the authority to launch a strike on a rival nation.
segments.texte: T-02:30 The United States doesn’t have a Dead Hand system… that we know of. A nuclear launch depends solely on the commander in chief. No one else has the authority to launch a strike on a rival nation. It’s a weight that no other person can carry.

segments.resume: In November 1979 NORAD computers showed hundreds of Russian missiles heading for the US, bombers were put on alert and threat conferences were called for six minutes. Backup radars showed empty skies because a technician had uploaded a realistic war game into the live system.
segments.texte: T-02:00 The American war machine grinds forward. Generals whisper prayers, the President clasps his hands. America is at nuclear war. And stopping it is almost impossible. In November 1979, the early warning computers at NORAD suddenly lit up. Russia had launched a nuclear strike. Hundreds of missiles were heading right for the U.S. Threat assessment conferences were called immediately. Tactical bombers were on high alert, sitting on the tarmac of America’s air bases. For 6 minutes, the U.S. military was ready to respond. Before the President made his decision, analysts checked the backup radars. The skies were empty. A technician had accidentally uploaded a realistic war game into the live, operational computer. The system couldn’t tell the difference between a simulation and real life. Unfortunately for the President, this is very much real.

segments.titre: The three-tier menu: limited, selected and major attack options
segments.resume: The President confirms his identity and chooses among Limited Attack Options, Selected Attack Options and Major Attack Options. Limited strikes risk looking like a first wave and triggering the other side's six-minute window, selected options signal war, and major options hit thousands of targets, about 6,500 installations in 1971.
segments.texte: T-01:00 The President stares at the Football as he utters the Biscuit codes down the line. His identity is confirmed. He has seconds to choose from a 3 tiered menu of death. At the bottom are Limited Attack Options: a small number of warheads directed at specific military targets. The strategic logic is to hit something precise, demonstrate capability, and invite the other side to stop before the world burns. The fatal problem, from the enemy’s perspective, a few incoming warheads look like the opening wave of a larger strike. It only triggers the same 6 minute decision window on the opposite side. In the middle are Selected Attack Options: a broader strike against regional military forces, naval assets, and military infrastructure. This signals the intent to launch a war, not necessarily a nuclear one. At the top are Major Attack Options: Launching thousands of warheads against thousands of targets simultaneously. In 1971, that list included some 6,500 installations. This is the option that decapitates the enemy leadership, command posts and nuclear forces in one fell swoop. The entire infrastructure of a civilization, methodically eliminated. He makes his selection… and signs the death warrant for millions.

segments.titre: Emergency Action Message and the launch
segments.resume: The President's order becomes an Emergency Action Message sent to submarines, silos and bombers, where two-person crews verify it and turn their keys with no latitude to question it, as Bruce Blair says. The missiles launch, the order cannot be recalled, and the six-minute window has worked perfectly.
segments.texte: T-00:30 This is the moment the President’s voice becomes an Emergency Action Message. The encrypted command is simultaneously sent to submarines, missile silos, and bomber crew pilots on standby across the planet. Two-person crews at missile silos and aboard submarines independently verify the message. They physically turn their launch keys and the weapons. They don’t bother calling you back or asking for confirmation. As nuclear expert Bruce Blair said, “There’s really no latitude to question an order” The authentication chain is already complete. T-00:00 The missiles roar out the silos and into the air. What happens next is all down to physics…and fate. The missiles are on their way. It’s an order that can’t be taken back. The 6 minute window worked perfectly. There’s nothing to do but wait…

segments.titre: Outro: Why Nuclear Armageddon is Unstoppable
segments.resume: The Football is described as only the trigger mechanism, and viewers are pointed to another video, 'Why Nuclear Armageddon is Unstoppable', about what happens once missiles are in the air.
segments.texte: The Football is just the trigger mechanism. Watch ‘Why Nuclear Armageddon is Unstoppable’ to understand that once the missiles are in the air, humanity is doomed. Or click on this.
